title: Anahat Singh Stuns Eight-Time World Champion El Sherbini at Silicon Valley Open
excerpt: The 18-year-old Indian beat top seed and world No. 3 Nour El Sherbini 11-8, 11-8, 11-7 in 30 minutes in Redwood City to reach the quarter-finals of the $143,500 PSA Gold event.
body:
• India's Anahat Singh, 18, beat eight-time world champion and top seed Nour El Sherbini 11-8, 11-8, 11-7 in 30 minutes at the Silicon Valley Open in Redwood City.
  • The straight-games win in the second round put Anahat into the quarter-finals of the $143,500 PSA Gold event — the biggest win of her professional career.
  • El Sherbini, the world No. 3 from Egypt, has won eight world titles, equalling Nicol David's record; Anahat had never faced her before.
  • Anahat reached the match by beating Egypt's Nour Aboulmakarim 11-8, 11-8, 12-10 in the opening round, and had earlier become the first Indian to win a women's singles silver in squash at the Asian Games.

Eighteen-year-old Anahat Singh produced the biggest win of her career on Wednesday, defeating eight-time world champion Nour El Sherbini 11-8, 11-8, 11-7 in just 30 minutes at the Silicon Valley Open in Redwood City, California. The straight-games victory over the top-seeded Egyptian sent the Indian into the quarter-finals of the $143,500 PSA Gold event, The Times of India reported.

El Sherbini arrived as the clear favourite: a world No. 3 whose eight world titles equal Nicol David's record, and a player who has held the world No. 1 ranking for extended periods and won four British Opens. Anahat, by contrast, was facing her for the first time. She won all three games by the same controlled pattern — 11-8, 11-8, then 11-7 to close it out — in a second-round match that lasted half an hour, a scoreline also reported by Inshorts.

"I grew up watching every single match of hers."

— Anahat Singh, on Nour El Sherbini, via The Times of India

A Rapid Rise Meets Its Biggest Test

Anahat, born in New Delhi on 13 March 2008, turned professional in 2023 and has risen to around the world top 15-17, according to The Times of India. Earlier in 2026 she became India's first World Junior champion — the first non-Egyptian winner since 2010 — and claimed a women's singles silver at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, the first Indian to do so. She is coached by former world No. 1 Gregory Gaultier alongside Saurav Ghosal and Stephane Galifi, and has already collected multiple PSA titles while becoming the youngest Asian player to break into the top 20.

That trajectory explains why this result matters beyond one evening in California. Junior titles and an Asian Games medal mark a prospect; a straight-games win over the most decorated active player in the women's game, at a Gold-level PSA event, marks a senior breakthrough. El Sherbini has defined the top of women's squash for a decade, and Egyptian players have long set the standard Anahat's generation is measured against.

How She Got to the Match

Anahat had eased into the second round by beating Egypt's Nour Aboulmakarim in the opening round — 11-8, 11-8, 12-10 in 31 minutes on the tournament's first day. That set up the first meeting of her career with El Sherbini, a player she said she had grown up watching. There was no sign of that deference on court: the scoreline never required a fourth game, and the third game, at 11-7, was the most decisive of the three.

What Comes Next

Anahat now plays a quarter-final at an event that runs from 20 to 24 October in Redwood City. A further win would take her into the semi-finals of a PSA Gold tournament — territory no Indian teenager has occupied — and would add ranking points that could push her further into the world's top group. The timing adds weight to the run: squash is preparing for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028, and results like this one, on American soil against the game's established hierarchy, are the clearest evidence yet that Anahat will arrive at those Games as a contender rather than a participant. For Indian squash, long carried by a small group of senior players, her win in Silicon Valley is a generational signal.
